Strengthen create-level work for slide 14: Remove some scaffolding from iteration design activity—provide project description and constraints but let students determine their own iteration structure, feedback mechanisms, and feature sequencing without guided questions.

Add artifact creation to slide 9: Include activity where students create Product Backlog and Sprint Backlog for a given scenario, write Definition of Done for specific project type, or evaluate whether provided artifacts meet transparency requirements.

Insert cumulative case study (new slide after 20): Present complex scenario requiring students to design complete agile approach: assign Scrum roles, write 5 user stories, plan 3 iterations, select XP practices, justify methodology choice, and identify quality risks—integrating all objectives.

Enhance slide 13 with analysis activity: Give students a quality problem scenario (e.g., frequent production bugs, slow feature delivery) and have them analyze which XP practice combinations would address root causes, explaining reinforcement relationships.

Add reflection prompts to hands-on activities: After TDD exercises (slides 11-12), include explicit reflection questions requiring students to analyze how the practice changed their design decisions or evaluate when TDD overhead is justified vs. when simpler testing suffices.

Strengthen evaluation in slide 6: After students evaluate the two team approaches, add second part where they must design hybrid approach combining elements of both, justifying which agile values they prioritize and which traditional elements they retain for the startup context.

slides.title: Lecture 9: Agile Development Methods and Practices

blocks.content: Lecture 9: Agile Development Methods and Practices

content.title: Your Agile Hypothesis
content.description: Consider a project you've worked on (class, personal, work). What was the biggest challenge: changing requirements, unclear goals, technical risks, or tight deadlines? Write down: (1) Which agile practice might have helped most—daily standups, iterative releases, TDD, or user stories? (2) Why that specific practice addresses your challenge. No wrong answers—we'll revisit your hypothesis at lecture end to evaluate if you'd change your choice.

slides.speakerNotes: This opening primes students to evaluate agile practices against real problems rather than passively receiving definitions. By committing to a hypothesis early, they'll actively test it against concepts throughout the lecture. The revisit promise creates cognitive tension supporting deeper engagement with methodology selection and evaluation objectives. Their written hypotheses become artifacts for analyzing how their understanding evolved, supporting the deck's apply-evaluate focus while addressing the create-level gap through personal synthesis.

slides.title: Your Agile Journey: From Concepts to Practice

items: Apply Scrum framework to organize real project scenarios
Implement XP practices through hands-on TDD exercises
Create user stories meeting INVEST criteria with peer review
Design iteration cycles for projects with specific constraints
Evaluate and justify methodology selection for case studies

content.title: Design Your Learning Path
content.description: Scenario: Your team has 8 weeks to build a mobile app prototype using agile. Draft a learning plan: Which 3 objectives will you master first and why? For each, identify one concrete deliverable you'll create today (e.g., 'Create user stories' → write 5 stories for login feature). Sketch your iteration timeline showing when you'll apply each skill. Compare plans with neighbor—did you sequence differently?

slides.speakerNotes: This activity elevates the slide from understand to create-level by requiring students to design their own learning strategy rather than passively rating abilities. Students must synthesize objectives into a coherent plan, prioritize based on dependencies, and create concrete deliverables—mirroring how they'll design iteration cycles later (slide 14). The neighbor comparison introduces peer evaluation of different sequencing choices. This primes students for the deck's apply-dominant approach while addressing the create-level gap. Their plans become reference points during hands-on activities, supporting metacognitive monitoring of actual vs. planned skill development.

slides.title: The Software Crisis: Why Agile Emerged

items: 1990s reality: 70% of projects failed, over budget, or late
Waterfall assumption: Requirements stable, predictable delivery
Market reality: Customer needs changed during 18+ month cycles
Consequence: Delivered software obsolete before release

content.title: Analyze the Mismatch
content.description: Given scenario: E-commerce startup plans 24-month waterfall project. Month 18: competitor launches mobile-first checkout. Your analysis: (1) Why does waterfall fail here? (2) Which agile principle addresses this? (3) How would 2-week iterations change the outcome? Write your diagnosis, then compare with neighbor.

slides.speakerNotes: Present the crisis as a methodology-context mismatch, not waterfall failure. After students analyze the scenario, reveal that agile emerged from practitioners facing exactly this problem. Key insight: methodology selection depends on requirement stability and feedback urgency. Connect their diagnosis to upcoming Agile Manifesto values—'responding to change over following a plan' directly addresses this scenario. This analysis primes students for the evaluation objective requiring methodology selection for different contexts. Transition to timeline showing how practitioners experimented with solutions.

slides.title: Evolution Timeline: Waterfall to Agile

content.prompt: Create a horizontal timeline showing software development methodology evolution: 1970s (Waterfall - sequential phases with downward arrows), 1980s (Iterative models - circular arrows), 1990s (Lightweight methods - Scrum, XP icons), 2001 (Agile Manifesto - document icon with 4 values), 2010s-Present (Scaled Agile, DevOps - network diagram). Use distinct colors for each era and include small representative icons.

content.title: Evaluate Methodology Fit
content.description: Three scenarios: (A) Banking system migration, strict regulatory compliance, fixed requirements. (B) Mobile app startup, evolving market, weekly user feedback. (C) NASA spacecraft software, safety-critical, 5-year timeline. For each: Select methodology from timeline (waterfall, iterative, or agile). Justify with 2 specific reasons based on project characteristics. Identify 1 risk if wrong methodology chosen. Write answers, then discuss.

slides.speakerNotes: Present timeline first, then launch evaluation activity. This directly addresses the 'select appropriate methodologies for different contexts' objective at evaluate level. After students work individually, facilitate brief discussion revealing: A likely suits waterfall (stable requirements, compliance documentation), B needs agile (uncertainty, rapid feedback), C may blend approaches (safety needs rigor, long timeline allows iteration). Emphasize no single right answer—justification quality matters. Connect choices to upcoming Manifesto values: their reasoning should reflect understanding that methodology matches project uncertainty and change frequency. Transition by noting the 2001 Manifesto codified principles they just applied intuitively.

slides.title: The Agile Manifesto: Four Core Values

items: Individuals and interactions > Processes and tools
Working software > Comprehensive documentation
Customer collaboration > Contract negotiation
Responding to change > Following a plan

blocks.content: While there is value in the items on the right, we value the items on the left more.

content.title: Evaluate and Design Methodology Approach
content.description: Scenario: E-commerce startup, 3-month MVP deadline, evolving requirements. Team A: 3-week requirements phase, fixed-price contract, monthly status reports, change control board. Team B: 1-week sprints, on-site customer, daily standups, flexible scope. (1) Evaluate each approach against all four values—which values does each honor or violate? (2) Design a hybrid approach: select elements from both teams, justify which values you prioritize and why certain traditional practices might still be needed.

slides.speakerNotes: Present values, then launch evaluation activity targeting evaluate and create levels. Students must evaluate two approaches against all four values, then create hybrid methodology justifying prioritization decisions. Expected reasoning: Team B aligns with agile values; Team A follows traditional approach but may offer risk mitigation through contracts. Hybrid might include sprints with lightweight contracts, daily standups with minimal documentation for compliance. Debrief emphasizes no single right answer—justification quality and value alignment matter. This directly supports methodology selection objective at evaluate level and prepares for next slide's concrete practice scenarios.

slides.title: Agile Values in Practice

items: Individuals & Interactions: Daily standup vs. status reports
Working Software: Demo vs. design document
Customer Collaboration: Product Owner on team vs. quarterly reviews
Responding to Change: Adapt backlog vs. change request forms

content.title: Evaluate and Design Hybrid Methodology
content.description: Scenario: Healthcare startup, 4-month MVP, evolving requirements, regulatory compliance needed. Team A: 3-week requirements phase, fixed contract, monthly reports, change control. Team B: 1-week sprints, on-site customer, daily standups, flexible scope. (1) Evaluate each against all four values—which does each honor or violate? (2) Design hybrid methodology: select elements from both, justify which values you prioritize for this context and which traditional practices you retain for compliance.

slides.speakerNotes: Activity targets evaluate and create levels, supporting methodology selection objective. Students evaluate two approaches against values, then create hybrid solution balancing agility with regulatory needs. Expected reasoning: Team B aligns with agile values; Team A offers compliance documentation. Hybrid might include 2-week sprints with lightweight compliance artifacts, daily standups with audit trails, customer collaboration within regulatory constraints. Debrief emphasizes justification quality and context-appropriate value prioritization. No single right answer—trade-off analysis matters. Connects to Scrum framework next, showing how specific practices operationalize these values.

slides.title: Scrum Framework Overview

items: 3 Roles: Product Owner, Scrum Master, Development Team
3 Artifacts: Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog, Increment
5 Events: Sprint, Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review, Sprint Retrospective
Foundation: Transparency, Inspection, Adaptation

content.title: Design Complete Scrum Implementation
content.description: Scenario: Campus food delivery mobile app. 5 developers, 1 designer, 4-month MVP timeline, evolving student feedback. Design your Scrum approach: (1) Create role structure—who fills each role and why might you need external stakeholders? (2) Design your sprint cadence and justify the length based on project constraints. (3) Create 6-8 prioritized backlog items reflecting MVP scope. (4) Plan first sprint goal and analyze how transparency/inspection/adaptation will manage requirement evolution. Present one coherent implementation strategy.

slides.speakerNotes: Activity elevated to create-level by removing scaffolding and requiring coherent strategy design rather than filling blanks. Students must synthesize role assignments, sprint structure, backlog prioritization, and pillar application into unified implementation plan. Expected decisions: external PO representing students, SM from team, 2-week sprints balancing feedback cycles with development rhythm, backlog prioritizing core ordering/payment flows. Debrief focuses on justification quality and internal consistency—does sprint length align with feedback needs? Does role structure enable transparency? Connects to next slide's detailed role exploration, showing how design decisions impact team dynamics.

slides.title: Scrum Roles and Interactions

items: Product Owner: Maximizes value, manages/prioritizes backlog, defines acceptance criteria
Scrum Master: Removes impediments, coaches team, facilitates events, shields from disruption
Development Team: Self-organizing, cross-functional, commits to sprint goals, delivers increment
Collaboration: PO clarifies requirements ↔ Team asks questions; SM coaches ↔ Team provides feedback

content.title: Design Role Structure for Complex Context
content.description: Scenario: 20-person product development (3 interdependent features, shared codebase, regulatory compliance needs, distributed across 2 time zones). Design your role structure: How many teams? How many Product Owners and why? Will Scrum Masters serve multiple teams or dedicate to one? How will you handle cross-team dependencies and architectural decisions? Justify each choice using Scrum principles (self-organization, transparency, encapsulation of responsibilities). Present coherent organizational design.

slides.speakerNotes: Activity elevated to create-level by requiring organizational design rather than analyzing violations. Students must synthesize role structure for scaled Scrum context, making architectural decisions about team composition, PO allocation, and coordination mechanisms. Expected decisions: 2-3 teams with dedicated SMs, single PO or PO + domain proxies, architecture guild for technical alignment. Debrief focuses on tradeoff analysis—does structure enable autonomy while maintaining coherence? How do role boundaries scale? Connects to next slide's artifacts discussion, showing how role design impacts backlog management and transparency across teams.

slides.title: Scrum Artifacts: Transparency Through Visibility

items: Product Backlog: Ordered list of all desired work
Sprint Backlog: Selected items + plan for current sprint
Increment: Potentially shippable product at sprint end
Definition of Done: Shared quality standard
All artifacts visible to entire team and stakeholders

slides.speakerNotes: Explain the flow: Product Backlog → Sprint Backlog → Increment. Emphasize 'potentially shippable'—the increment must meet the Definition of Done, even if not actually released. Give DoD example: 'Code reviewed, tests pass, documentation updated, deployed to staging.' Relate to earlier lectures: DoD can include DbC assertions verified, coding standards met, design patterns properly applied.

slides.title: Sprint Cycle: Design Your Sprint Strategy

content.prompt: Create a circular diagram showing a 2-week sprint cycle. Clockwise from top: 'Sprint Planning' (4h) → 'Daily Scrum' (15 min, small circles around arc) → 'Development Work' (largest arc) → 'Sprint Review' (2h) → 'Sprint Retrospective' (1.5h) → back to Sprint Planning. Center shows 'Sprint Goal' and 'Increment'. Use clock icons for time-boxing.

content.title: Create: Design Sprint Structure
content.instructions: Your 6-person team builds a healthcare compliance app (HIPAA regulations require audit trails, security reviews). Historical velocity: 18-22 pts/sprint. Product Backlog has 12 stories (3-13 pts each) with dependencies. Design your first 3 sprints: select stories for each, sequence them considering dependencies and compliance needs, write sprint goals, and specify when regulatory reviews occur. Justify your iteration strategy.
content.deliverable: 3-sprint plan with story assignments, goals, review points, and strategic justification explaining dependency management and compliance integration

slides.speakerNotes: Walk through sprint cycle diagram emphasizing time-boxing and event purposes. Launch design activity requiring students to create multi-sprint strategy rather than just select stories for one sprint. This elevates to create-level by demanding synthesis of dependencies, regulatory constraints, and iteration planning. Students must design their own sequencing logic and justify trade-offs. Debrief solutions: How did compliance reviews affect sprint boundaries? Did anyone front-load risky stories vs. building foundational features first? Connect to objective of designing iterative cycles with real-world constraints.

slides.title: Extreme Programming: Implement Core Practices

items: 5 Values: Communication, Simplicity, Feedback, Courage, Respect
Pair Programming: Two developers, one keyboard—driver codes, navigator reviews
Test-Driven Development: Red (failing test) → Green (minimal code) → Refactor
Continuous Integration: Merge code multiple times daily, automated tests verify
Collective Code Ownership: Any team member can improve any code

content.title: Apply: Pair Programming + TDD
content.instructions: Pair with a neighbor. Person A writes a failing test for a function that validates passwords (min 8 chars, 1 uppercase, 1 digit). Person B writes minimal code to pass. Switch roles: Person B writes test for edge case (empty string), Person A implements. Discuss: How did pairing catch errors? Did TDD clarify requirements?
content.deliverable: Test code + implementation + 2 observations about pairing/TDD benefits

slides.speakerNotes: Introduce XP as engineering complement to Scrum's project management. Walk through values and practices briefly. Then launch hands-on exercise: students experience pair programming and TDD simultaneously. Monitor pairs—common issues: driver ignoring navigator, writing implementation before test. Debrief: How did real-time code review improve quality? Did writing tests first clarify expected behavior? Connect to earlier OO principles: TDD supports correctness, pairing spreads knowledge (reduces key-person risk). This applies XP practices directly, elevating from understand to apply level and addressing the implementation objective gap.

slides.title: Test-Driven Development: Analyze Design Impact

content.prompt: Create a circular flow diagram showing TDD Red-Green-Refactor cycle. Three nodes with arrows: (1) 'RED' (red X icon) - 'Write failing test first', (2) 'GREEN' (green checkmark) - 'Minimal code to pass', (3) 'REFACTOR' (blue wrench) - 'Improve design, tests still pass'. Clockwise arrows between nodes. Add small code icons at each stage showing test → function → improved function.

content.title: Analyze: TDD's Design Influence
content.instructions: Implement email validator two ways. FIRST: Write implementation directly (no tests), supporting formats: user@domain.com, user+tag@domain.co.uk. SECOND: Use TDD—write 4 tests (valid basic, valid with tag, invalid missing @, invalid no domain), then implement. Compare: Which version has better modularity? Which handles edge cases? Analyze how writing tests first changed your design decisions. Evaluate: When would TDD overhead NOT be justified?
content.deliverable: Both implementations + 3-sentence analysis of design differences + 1 scenario where TDD overhead isn't worth it

slides.speakerNotes: Students experience TDD's design impact by comparing test-first vs. code-first approaches for same problem. This elevates from apply to analyze—they must examine how TDD shaped their design choices, coupling, and edge case handling. Monitor for superficial comparisons; push students to identify structural differences. Debrief common findings: TDD version often more modular, testable functions. Discussion on when TDD overhead isn't justified (throwaway prototypes, simple scripts) addresses evaluate-level thinking. Connects to create-level iteration design objective by showing how TDD practice influences development cycle structure and quality gates.

slides.title: XP Practices: Reinforcing Quality

content.prompt: Create a mind map with 'XP Practices' at center, branches radiating outward showing practice relationships: (1) 'TDD' connects to 'Refactoring' and 'Simple Design', (2) 'Continuous Integration' connects to 'Collective Ownership' and 'Coding Standards', (3) 'Pair Programming' connects to 'TDD' and 'Collective Ownership', (4) 'Small Releases' connects to 'CI' and 'Customer Feedback'. Use arrows to show how practices support each other. Include small icons for each practice.

slides.speakerNotes: Show how XP practices reinforce each other—this is a system, not isolated techniques. For example: TDD enables confident refactoring, refactoring maintains simple design, CI requires collective ownership, pair programming spreads knowledge enabling collective ownership. Emphasize sustainable pace: 40-hour weeks, no heroics. Relate to course themes: these practices support extendibility, reusability, correctness from earlier lectures.

slides.title: Iterative vs. Incremental Development

content.prompt: Create a comparison diagram with two sections. Top: 'Waterfall' showing sequential boxes (Requirements → Design → Implementation → Testing → Deployment) with no overlap. Bottom: 'Iterative-Incremental' showing 4 overlapping cycles, each containing mini-phases (Plan → Design → Code → Test). Show growing functionality with each iteration: Iteration 1 (small feature set), Iteration 2 (medium), Iteration 3 (larger), Iteration 4 (complete). Use stacked blocks to show incremental growth and circular arrows to show iterative refinement.

content.title: Design Your Iteration Plan
content.instructions: You're building a healthcare patient portal. Constraints: 4-month timeline, regulatory review required every 6 weeks, team velocity 20 pts/sprint, monthly stakeholder demos. Design your development plan: (1) Specify iteration length (1-4 weeks) and total number of iterations, (2) Map which features to build in each iteration (login, appointments, records, prescriptions), (3) Identify feedback points and regulatory checkpoints, (4) Justify your iteration length choice with 2 specific reasons.

slides.speakerNotes: First clarify concepts: Iterative = refining through cycles, Incremental = building piece by piece. Agile combines both. Then transition to activity: students design custom iteration strategy, not just apply template. This requires synthesizing constraints (regulatory reviews, demos, velocity) into coherent plan. Circulate to check: Are iterations too long (risk)? Too short (overhead)? Do regulatory reviews align with iteration boundaries? Debrief: Compare 2-week vs 3-week choices, discuss tradeoffs between feedback frequency and feature completeness per iteration.

slides.title: Managing Technical Debt

items: Technical Debt: Shortcuts taken for speed, require future rework
Causes: Tight deadlines, changing requirements, learning
Impact: Slower velocity, increased bugs, harder to change
Management: Track debt, allocate refactoring time (20% per sprint)
Spike Solutions: Time-boxed research to reduce uncertainty

content.title: Identify and Prioritize Technical Debt
content.instructions: Review this code snippet: a user authentication module with hard-coded credentials, no input validation, duplicated logic across 3 methods, and missing error handling. Tasks: (1) Identify 4 specific technical debt items, (2) Estimate 'interest cost' for each (low/medium/high impact on velocity), (3) Prioritize which 2 to address first in next sprint with justification, (4) Propose a 2-day spike to investigate OAuth integration—what questions should it answer?

slides.speakerNotes: Use financial metaphor: debt is like a loan—useful short-term but accrues interest. Activity targets analyze-level: students must identify debt in realistic code, not just define the concept. Circulate to check: Are they distinguishing between high-interest debt (security issues, duplicated logic) vs. low-interest (minor style inconsistencies)? Do spike questions address uncertainty (OAuth providers, token storage, migration path)? Debrief: Compare prioritization choices. Emphasize strategic debt is acceptable if tracked and repaid. Connect to XP practice of sustainable pace and refactoring.

slides.title: User Stories: INVEST Criteria

items: Independent: Can be developed in any order
Negotiable: Details emerge through conversation
Valuable: Provides clear benefit to user/stakeholder
Estimable: Team can estimate size/effort
Small: Fits within one iteration
Testable: Clear acceptance criteria

content.title: Write and Critique User Stories
content.instructions: Create 3 user stories with acceptance criteria for a library management system feature: book reservation. Use role-feature-benefit format. Include 2 acceptance criteria per story. Then peer-review a partner's stories: check each against all 6 INVEST criteria, identify 2 violations or weaknesses, suggest specific improvements. Be ready to justify your INVEST assessment.

slides.speakerNotes: Brief INVEST overview using bullets, then transition to creation activity. This targets the create-level objective for writing user stories. Circulate to check: Are stories in proper format (As a [role], I want [feature], so that [benefit])? Are acceptance criteria testable and specific? During peer review, listen for INVEST reasoning—students should cite specific criteria violations like 'Not Small—spans multiple sprints' or 'Not Testable—vague criteria.' Debrief by sharing strong examples and common pitfalls. Emphasize acceptance criteria define 'done' and connect to testing practices covered in XP slides.

slides.title: Sprint Planning Process

content.prompt: Two-column flow chart. Left 'Part 1: What?': Product Backlog → PO presents priorities → Team asks questions → Team selects stories (based on velocity/capacity) → Sprint Goal. Right 'Part 2: How?': Selected stories → Break into tasks → Identify dependencies → Estimate hours → Sprint Backlog (stories + tasks). Use arrows and icons.

content.title: Conduct Sprint Planning
content.instructions: Team of 4. Given: Product backlog with 8 user stories (3-8 pts each), team velocity 18 pts, capacity 120 hours this sprint. Part 1: Select stories to commit (justify using velocity). Create one cohesive sprint goal. Part 2: Pick your top story, break into 4-6 technical tasks with hour estimates. Identify one dependency. Present: sprint goal, committed stories, task breakdown.
content.deliverable: Sprint goal + committed stories + task breakdown for one story

slides.speakerNotes: Brief diagram walkthrough: Part 1 determines what (PO presents, team commits based on capacity), Part 2 determines how (task breakdown, dependencies). Then launch activity simulating real planning. Circulate to check: Are teams respecting velocity limits? Is sprint goal cohesive (not just list of stories)? Are tasks technical and granular (3-8 hours each)? Debrief common issues: over-committing, vague goals like 'finish stories,' missing dependencies. Emphasize team self-organizes and commits—PO doesn't assign. Connect to slide 10's backlog prioritization and slide 16's story quality.

slides.title: Agile vs. Traditional: Choosing the Right Approach

items: Requirements: Agile (emergent) vs. Traditional (defined upfront)
Planning: Agile (adaptive) vs. Traditional (comprehensive)
Control: Agile (empirical) vs. Traditional (defined process)
Risk: Agile (early delivery) vs. Traditional (upfront analysis)
Best for Agile: Innovation, changing needs, small teams
Best for Traditional: Stable requirements, safety-critical, compliance

slides.speakerNotes: Present balanced comparison—neither approach is universally superior. Agile excels with uncertainty and change; traditional works for predictable, well-understood domains. Give examples: Agile for startup mobile app (changing market), Traditional for medical device (regulatory requirements). Mention hybrid approaches: agile development with waterfall documentation for compliance. Emphasize: tailor methodology to context, don't follow dogmatically. Ask students to consider their semester projects.

slides.title: Agile Supporting Software Quality

items: Correctness: TDD verifies behavior, DbC verifies contracts
Robustness: CI catches integration issues, small increments limit risk
Extendibility: Refactoring prevents decay, SOLID principles guide structure
Reusability: Collective ownership spreads knowledge, patterns emerge

content.title: Quality Practice Analysis
content.instructions: Analyze this scenario: A team's code has 40% test coverage, no CI pipeline, and duplicated validation logic across 5 classes. (1) Identify which quality attributes are at risk. (2) Select 3 agile practices to address the issues. (3) For each practice, explain how it improves a specific quality attribute and estimate adoption effort (low/medium/high). (4) Prioritize the practices—which should be introduced first and why?

slides.speakerNotes: This activity elevates understanding to analysis and evaluation. Students must diagnose quality problems (low coverage risks correctness, no CI risks robustness, duplication harms extendibility), then evaluate which practices address them. Prioritization requires justifying trade-offs between impact and effort. Sample solution: (1) TDD for correctness (medium effort), (2) CI for robustness (high effort), (3) Refactoring for extendibility (low effort). Prioritize refactoring first (quick win), then TDD (builds discipline), finally CI (infrastructure investment). Debrief: How do practices reinforce each other? This synthesizes agile practices with quality attributes from earlier lectures.

slides.title: Agile in Object-Oriented Development

items: Evolutionary Design: Classes emerge through refactoring, not upfront
TDD drives interface design: Tests first → loose coupling (DIP)
Refactor to Patterns: Apply when needed (YAGNI), not speculatively
Continuous refactoring maintains SOLID principles over time

content.title: Design Evolution Exercise
content.instructions: Scenario: You're building a notification system. Initially, only email notifications are needed. (1) Design a simple class structure (just class names and key methods). (2) New requirement: Add SMS notifications. Refactor your design—what changes? Which SOLID principle guides you? (3) Third requirement: Log all notifications. Apply a design pattern. Which pattern and why? (4) Reflect: How did TDD (testing each notification type separately) influence your coupling decisions?

slides.speakerNotes: This activity elevates the slide from understanding integration to applying evolutionary design. Students start simple (single EmailNotifier class), then refactor when requirements change (extract INotifier interface for SMS, applying Open-Closed Principle). The logging requirement prompts Decorator or Observer pattern. Debrief focuses on how TDD encourages designing for testability (dependency injection, interfaces), which naturally leads to SOLID compliance. Emphasize: agile doesn't mean no design—it means design emerges from real needs, validated by tests. This synthesizes OO principles with agile practices, addressing the implementation objective by having students actually design and refactor.

slides.title: Summary: Agile Ecosystem

content.prompt: Create a comprehensive infographic showing the agile ecosystem. Center: 'Agile Manifesto' (4 values). Inner ring: 'Methodologies' (Scrum, XP, Kanban icons). Middle ring: 'Practices' (TDD, CI, Pair Programming, Refactoring, User Stories icons). Outer ring: 'Benefits' (Faster delivery, Higher quality, Better collaboration, Adaptability). Use concentric circles with connecting lines showing relationships. Include small representative icons and use a cohesive color scheme.

slides.speakerNotes: Synthesize the lecture: Agile Manifesto provides values, methodologies (Scrum, XP) provide frameworks, practices (TDD, CI, refactoring) implement the frameworks, benefits (speed, quality, collaboration) result. Emphasize agile as a mindset, not just practices. Success requires: team commitment, organizational support, customer collaboration, continuous improvement through retrospectives. Preview next steps: students should apply these techniques in their projects. Mention future trends: DevOps, continuous delivery, agile at scale.

slides.title: Key Takeaways and Next Steps

items: Agile is a mindset: Embrace change, value individuals, focus on working software
Scrum provides project framework; XP provides engineering practices
Quality built-in: TDD, CI, refactoring prevent defects
Iterative + Incremental: Deliver value early, refine continuously
Choose methodology based on context: requirements stability, team size, criticality
Apply in your projects: User stories, sprint planning, TDD, retrospectives

slides.speakerNotes: Conclude with actionable takeaways. Emphasize that students should apply these techniques in semester projects: write user stories, conduct sprint planning, practice TDD, hold retrospectives. Remind them that agile integrates with earlier course topics: supports OO development, complements DbC, enhances quality attributes. Encourage experimentation—agile is about continuous improvement. Assign exercises: write user stories for their projects, practice TDD, plan a sprint. Preview assessments: portfolio components, practical exams, case study analysis.

objectiveAlignments.objective: Understand the core values and principles of the Agile Manifesto and their impact on modern software development
objectiveAlignments.rationale: Slides 5-6 exceed expectations by requiring students to evaluate Team A vs Team B approaches against all four Manifesto values, then design hybrid methodologies with justified value prioritization. This demonstrates understanding through application and evaluation rather than passive explanation.

objectiveAlignments.objective: Apply the Scrum framework including roles, artifacts, and ceremonies to organize software projects
objectiveAlignments.rationale: Slides 7-10 and 17 require students to design complete Scrum implementations for realistic scenarios (campus food delivery app, 20-person distributed team, sprint planning simulation). Students create role structures, sprint cadences, backlog prioritization, and task breakdowns rather than just identifying Scrum components in examples.

objectiveAlignments.objective: Implement Extreme Programming (XP) practices to improve code quality and team collaboration
objectiveAlignments.rationale: Slides 11-12 provide hands-on implementation through pair programming + TDD exercise where students write actual test code and implementations. Slide 12 elevates to analyze level by comparing test-first vs code-first approaches to examine design impact. Activities require doing XP practices, not just describing them.

objectiveAlignments.objective: Design and execute iterative and incremental development cycles
objectiveAlignments.rationale: Slides 10 and 14 require students to design multi-sprint strategies and iteration plans for complex scenarios with regulatory constraints, dependencies, and stakeholder demos. Students must synthesize constraints into coherent iteration structures and justify sequencing decisions, directly addressing the create-level design objective.

objectiveAlignments.objective: Create effective user stories and conduct sprint planning sessions
objectiveAlignments.rationale: Slide 16 requires students to write 3 original user stories with acceptance criteria, then peer-review against INVEST criteria. Slide 17 simulates sprint planning where students select stories, create sprint goals, and break stories into tasks. Both activities involve creating artifacts rather than analyzing provided examples.

objectiveAlignments.objective: Compare and contrast agile versus traditional development approaches and select appropriate methodologies for different contexts
objectiveAlignments.rationale: Slides 4, 5-6, and 18 require methodology evaluation and selection. Slide 4 has students evaluate methodology fit for banking/startup/NASA scenarios with justification. Slides 5-6 require evaluating approaches against Manifesto values and designing hybrid methodologies. Slide 18 provides comparison framework. Activities demand justified selection based on context analysis.

gaps: Slide 9 (Scrum Artifacts) presents concepts at understand level without activity to apply artifact creation or analysis, creating passive learning gap in otherwise hands-on Scrum sequence

Slide 13 (XP Practices map) explains practice integration at understand level but misses opportunity for students to analyze how practices reinforce each other in specific scenarios or design practice adoption sequences

Slide 18 (Agile vs Traditional comparison) provides framework at understand level without requiring students to evaluate methodology selection for cases, despite this being explicit learning objective

Limited opportunities for students to evaluate trade-offs between competing agile practices or critique agile methodology limitations—most evaluation focuses on methodology selection rather than critical assessment of agile itself
No activities requiring students to create original agile process adaptations or evaluate when agile practices should be modified for specific organizational contexts beyond provided scenarios
suggestions: Slide 9: Add activity where students create Definition of Done for specific project type (e.g., mobile app vs embedded system), then evaluate how DoD affects sprint planning and increment acceptance—elevates from understand to create/evaluate

Slide 13: Replace passive mind map with activity requiring students to analyze a failing project scenario, diagnose which practice gaps caused problems, then design practice adoption sequence with justification of dependencies—elevates to analyze/create

Slide 18: Add case study activity where students evaluate 3 different project contexts (varying requirement stability, team size, criticality), select methodology for each with multi-criteria justification, and identify hybrid elements needed—aligns with evaluate-level objective

Add slide requiring students to critique agile methodology limitations: analyze scenarios where agile practices fail (e.g., distributed teams, safety-critical systems, fixed-bid contracts), evaluate which agile principles conflict with constraints, propose adaptations—develops critical evaluation skills

Slide 21-22: Replace passive summary with synthesis activity where students design agile adoption plan for realistic organization (e.g., traditional enterprise transitioning to agile), selecting which practices to introduce in which order, justifying sequencing based on organizational constraints and practice dependencies—creates capstone create-level synthesis

Consider adding reflection activity where students revisit their opening hypothesis from Slide 1, evaluate whether they would change their practice selection based on lecture content, and justify what new understanding influenced their thinking—closes metacognitive loop and reinforces evaluate-level learning
